To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a diffuse pollution hydrologic model can predict pesticide concentrations in rivers using precise data on farming and pesticide adsorption/degradation in soil.

precise model inputs obtained by collecting farming data from all farmers and measuring pesticide properties in paddy field soils can successfully verify a hydrological diffuse pollution model for predicting pesticide concentrations in river waters.

precise model inputs obtained from all paddy fields and pesticide properties in a catchment successfully verified the model and the model was sensitive to the farming schedule, but not to soil properties.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new approach for verifying a diffuse pollution hydrologic model and with the sensitivity analyses of the precise inputs obtained in this study.
the verification of a model to predict pesticide concentrations and the elucidation of processes significantly affecting pesticide concentrations in river waters using precise model inputs.
the verification of a diffuse pollution hydrology model for predicting pesticide concentrations in river waters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the timing of increases in river water concentrations of pesticides is determined by farming schedules, and that the magnitude of increases in river concentrations of pesticides is affected by rainfall events.

the timing of pesticide runoff from rice fields is affected mostly by the timing of pesticide application and the farming schedule and secondarily by pesticide adsorption and desorption, degradation, and rainfall events.
the timing of pesticide application, irrigation, and rainfall is more important than pesticide adsorption and soil degradation rates in determining the timing of pesticide runoff from rice fields.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a hydrological model can predict pesticide concentrations in rivers if it has precise model inputs.
the model can be used to predict pesticide concentrations if precise model inputs are available.

the model is able to reproduce the observed pesticide concentration in river water, and the model can be used to predict pesticide concentrations for various pesticide applications, rainfall events, and farming schedules.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a hydrological model can be verified by precise model inputs, even when the target catchments are large, if precise data sets on the farming and pesticide properties can be obtained.
the model inputs can be precisely estimated for large catchments, and the model can successfully predict pesticide concentrations in catchment runoff.
a diffuse pollution model that is able to reproduce the actual concentration of a target pesticide can be developed using precise model inputs.
